parent_headings: An effective multi-start iterated greedy algorithm to minimize makespan for the distributed permutation flowshop scheduling problem with preventive maintenance

content:
## A B S T R A C T
In recent years, distributed scheduling problems have been well studied for their close connection with multifactory production networks. However, the maintenance operations that are commonly carried out on a sys tem to restore it to a specific state are seldom taken into consideration. In this paper, we study a distributed permutation flowshop scheduling problem with preventive maintenance operation (PM/DPFSP). A multi-start iterated greedy (MSIG) algorithm is proposed to minimize the makespan. An improved heuristic is presented for the initialization and re-initialization by adding a dropout operation to NEH2 to generate solutions with a high level of quality and disperstiveness. A destruction phase with the tournament selection and a construction phase with an enhanced strategy are introduced to avoid local optima. A local search based on three effective operators is integrated into the MSIG to reinforce local neighborhood solution exploitation. In addition. a restart strategy is adpoted if a solution has not been improved in a certain number of consecutive iterations. We con ducted extensive experiments to test the performance of the presented MSIG. The computational results indicate that the presented MSIG has many promising advantages in solving the PM/DPFSP under consideration.

content:
## 1. Introduction
The distributed permutation flowshop scheduling problem (DPFSP) has attracted increasing attention (Fernandez-Viagas & Framinan, 2015; Pan et al., 2019) in the context of decentralized and globalized economy. A multi-factory production environment is becoming more and more common. In multi-factory production network, the total manufacture tasks are allocated among serval independent units, which brings great benefits to the enterprise, including higher production efficiency, lower production costs, better product quality, and so on (Behnamian & Ghomi, 2016). The DPFSP explores the production scheduling problem under the condition that companies have established factories in different locations.
DPFSP contains n jobs in the set $N = \{ 1 , 2 , . . . , n \}$ that is to be assigned to one factory out of a set of F identical factories $G = \left\{ 1 , 2 , . . . , F \right\}$ , in which each factory contains the same series of m machines $M = \{ 1 , 2 . .$ m}. It is assumed that all the machines are continuously available from the beginning to the end in the production process. Nevertheless, in the actual industrial production, reliability and maintainability decrease as the operation time of the machine increases (Rausand & Høyland, 2003). Generally, companies are aiming at a reliable production system with high availability performance. Therefore, maintenance operations are carried out on a system to restore it to a specific state (Birolini, 2013). There are two large types of maintenance operations: corrective main tenance (CM) and preventive maintenance (PM). The actions carried out after the failure has already occurred are referred to as CM. PM opera tions are carried out on machines before the breakdown or failure takes place. The purpose of PM operations is to increase equipment life and to enhance production management during production operations. The advantage of PM is that machines are always in good condition, thus reducing the risk of failures and avoiding the loss of failure. In industry, PM operations are widely used and planned to be conducted at pre defined time intervals without considering specific working conditions of equipment.
In this paper, the DPFSP with PM operation (PM/DPFSP) is consid ered. A complete schedule of the PM/DPFSP involves two subproblems: the assignment of jobs to F factories and the sequence of jobs in each factory. The PM/DPFSP is an NP-Hard problem as a variation of DPFSF (Naderi & Ruiz, 2010). The objective is to minimize the maximum complete time $C _ { m a x }$ among all the factories. In order to obtain solutions with both good quality and high efficiency, we propose a multi-start iterated greedy (MSIG) algorithm in this paper. The MSIG is a meta heuristic algorithm that obtains only one candidate solution in each iteration. To generate an initial solution with both good quality and diversity, we apply an improved NEH2 heuristic method with dropout operations. Then in the destruction and construction phases, a few jobs are randomly removed from the current solution and then greedily reinserted into new positions to explore neighboring solutions. After ward, we consider two operators to propose three local search methods to constitute an efficient local search procedure. Finally, we utilize a simulated annealing acceptance criterion and a restart strategy to pre vent local optimum. The purpose of the restart strategy is to reinitialize the current solution after it has not been improved for serval iterations.

## 2. Literature review The closely related literature can be divided into two categories: DPFSP and the scheduling problems with PM operation. In order to narrow the gap between academic research and practical applications, DPFSP has been studied for a long time as an extension of the permu tation flowshop scheduling problem (Maccarthy and Liu, 1993). Naderi and Ruiz (2010) first denoted DPFSP as $D P / p r m u / C _ { m a x } ,$ and proposed a total of 12 heuristic methods and two variable neighborhood descent (VND) algorithms. Following the initial work of Naderi and Ruiz (2010), many authors have studied more advanced algorithms in the last de cades. A hybrid genetic algorithm was presented by Gao and Chen (2011) to minimize the maximum completion time, where an efficient local search was utilized to explore neighboring solutions. Gao, Chen and Deng (2013) proposed a tabu algorithm with a novel tabu strategy. They utilized an enhanced local search method and a sub-sequence swapping method to generate neighborhood solutions. Lin. Ying and Huang (2013) modified the iterated greedy (IG) algorithm for the DPFSP. and proposed a destruction operator with a variable number of removed jobs and a simulated annealing algorithm with a sinking tem perature. Wang et al. (2013) proposed an effective estimation of distri. bution algorithm (EDA). They employed the earliest completion factory rule, and designed a probability model, and proposed four local search operators based on the problem characteristics. Naderi and Ruiz (2014) presented a scatter search (SS) procedure, which has seldom been explored for flowshop settings. The SS procedure was demonstrated to statistically outperform the other 11 algorithms in the experiments. Xu et al. (201 4) proposed a hybrid immune algorithm, where four different local search operators were used in a hybrid way within the frame of the immune algorithm. Fernandez-Viagas and Framinan (2015) developed a bounded-search IG algorithm for the DPESP In order to reduce the number of solutions to be evaluated. they studied the property of the problem to estimate the makespan of a factory when a new job is inserted. The effect of the bounded search method is that the compu tational time is discarded by 32.31% and the number of iterations is decreased by 11.68%. Bargaoui, Belkahla Driss and Gh´edira (2017) presented a chemical reaction optimization algorithm, in which a one point crossover and a greedy strategy are embedded to ameliorate the solution quality. Deng and Wang (2017) proposed a competitive mem: etic algorithm to solve the multi-objective DPFSP with makespan and total tardiness criteria. They employed two populations to optimize the two objectives and designed the interaction between the two pop ulations to balance the two obiectives. Ruiz. Pan and Naderi (2019) presented a simple two-stage iterated greedy (IG2S) algorithm with improved initialization, destruction, construction and local search procedures. Despite its simplicity, the IG2S significantly exceeds the other state-of-the-art algorithms in comparison. For the DPFSP with total flowtime optimization, Fernandezviagas, Perezgonzalez and Fra minan (2018) proposed eighteen constructive heuristics to generate feasible solutions with high quality in reasonable computational time and an evolutionary algorithm to further improve the so-obtained so lutions. Pan et al. (2019) Introduced three constructive heuristics and four metaheuristics to suit the needs of different CPU time demands and solution quality. There are also literatures proposed for other variations of the DPFSP. Rifai, Nguyen and Dawal (2016) gave a survey of the distributed reen trant permutation flowshop scheduling problem and developed a multiobjective adaptive large neighborhood search algorithm. Wang and Wang (2016) proposed a memetic algorithm for solving the distributed assembly permutation flowshop. Wang, Huang and Qin (2016) consid ered the DPFSP under machine breakdown with makespan criterion and proposed a fuzzy logic-based hybrid EDA. Zhang, Xing and Cao (2018) presented a hybrid discrete differential evolution (DDE) algorithm to deal with the distributed blocking flowshop scheduling problem (DBFSP) with makespan criterion. Pan et al. (2019) addressed a distributed assembly permutation flowshop scheduling problem in which each factory consists of a flowshop for part-processing and an assembly line for product-processing. Meng, Pan and Wang (2019) studied a DPFSP with customer order constraint. Jing et al. (2020) dealt with the DPFSP with due windows to minimize the total weighted earliness and tardiness. Huang, Pan and Gao (2020) extend the DPFSP by considering the sequence-dependent setup time (SDST). Zhao et al. (2020) presented an ensemble DDE algorithm for solving the DBFSP with makespan minimization. Meng and Pan (2021) solved a DPFSP with non-identical factories (DPFSP-NF) with lot-streaming and SDST considered. Lu et al. (2021) presented a knowledge-based multi-objec tive memetic optimization algorithm to minimizing makespan, negative social impact and total energy consumption of the DPFSP-NF. Wang and Wang (2020) applied a knowledge-based cooperative algorithm to address the energy-efficient scheduling of the DPFSP. Most recently, Huang et al. (2021) proposed three heuristic methods and an effective DABC algorithm for minimizing the makespan of the DPFSP with the machine-independent SDST. The corresponding literatures on the scheduling problem with PM operation are abundant as well. Ruiz, Garciadiaz and Maroto (2007) considered PM operation in a flowshop scheduling problem. They compared three PM policies and tested three heuristics and two meta heuristic methods. Extensive computational evaluations have given a result that the genetic algorithm (GA) and the ant colony optimization algorithm (ACO) are the two best algorithms. Yang, Hsu and Kuo (2008) considered a two-machine flowshop scheduling problem with a sepa rated maintenance constraint. According to their problem, the machine needs PM operations after it completes a certain amount of jobs rather than keeps working for a certain period of time. Wang and Yu (2010) proposed a filtered beam search based heuristic algorithm for solving a flexible job-shop scheduling problem with machine availability con straints. They studied a scheduling problem with both fixed and non fixed machine availability constraints in the flexible job-shop manufacturing environment. Naderi, Zandieh and Amimmayeri (2011) investigated a flexible flowshop scheduling with periodic PM operation on machines to minimize makespan. They applied a GA and an artificial immune system to solve the problem. Wong, Chan and Chung (2013) formulated a new scheduling problem with multiple resources and PM tasks as an integer-programming model and solved it by a GA approach. Xu and Yang (2013) studied a two-parallel-machines scheduling prob lem where one machine is periodically unavailable and jobs are nonpreemptive. They applied the classical longest processing time first (LPT) rule and the list scheduling (LS) rule for minimizing the makespan. Computational experiments showed that the LPT beat the LS. Lei and Liu (2020) applied an artificial bee colony (ABC) algorithm with a division for solving distributed unrelated parallel machines scheduling problems with PM operations. To generate solutions with high quality, they divided the whole swarm into one employed bee colony and three onlooker bee colonies, whose search strategy were different from each other. J.-y. As has been reviewed above, the DPFSP and the scheduling problems with PM operations have been widely studied in recent years. To the best of our knowledge, there is no existing literature on PM/DPFSP. Even though many high-performance algorithms have been developed, we are not aware of how well these existing algorithms perform on the PM/ DPFSP. Therefore, in this study, we propose an effective MSIG algorithm and compare it with the state-of-the-art algorithms from the literature by a comprehensive comparison.

## 3. DPFSP with PM operation
The PM/DPFSP can be depicted as follows. The set of jobs N is to be assigned to the factory set G. In each factory, all the jobs are processed on the machine set M in the order from machine 1 to machine m following the same route. Each machine i, i M, can only process one job simultaneously and each job $j , j \in N ,$ , can only be processed on one machine at one time. Each job j requires a certain amount of processing time on each machine $i ,$ which is described as $p _ { i , j } .$ All the jobs and ma chines are available for the process at time 0. In order to ensure the maintainability and reliability of a production system, PM operations are processed on all the machines periodically. The maintenance oper ation performed on machine i is described as $P M _ { i } , i \in M .$ The processing interval of PM is denoted as $I _ { i } ,$ which means that for each I units of processing time, machine i must be stopped for PM. The processing time of PM is denoted as $T _ { i \cdot }$ Once a job or a PM operation starts its processing on a machine, it cannot be interrupted.
The following example illustrates a solution of PM/DPFSP. Suppose that there is a set of ten jobs to be assigned to two factories each of which consists of two machines, that is, $m = 3 , n = 1 0$ and F = 2. The processing time of the jobs and PM operations are shown in Table 1.
Fig. 1 shows an optimal solution for the example without considering the PM operator, i.e. the original DPFSP. We obtain the optimal solu tions by enumerating all the feasible solutions. One of them ${ \mathrm { i } } s ,$ the job sequences at factory 0 and factory 1 being {8, 3, 4, 7, 1} and {6, 9, 3, 5, 0} respectively. The makespan of this solution is 36. In Fig. 2, the scheduling criterion of the PM operations is applied to the previous optimal solution. It can be seen that the PM operations disrupted the tight schedule. There is plenty of idle time on machine 2 in each factory, which leads to larger completion time. Take job 2 in factory 1 on ma chine 1 for example to illustrate the PM operation, the accumulated total processing time before job 2 starts is $p _ { 1 , 6 } + p _ { 1 , 9 } = 2 + 2 = 4 ,$ which is no larger than the interval time of PM operations on machine 2. While job 2 has a processing time of $p _ { 1 , 2 } = 9$ on machine 1, resulting in an accu mulated total processing time of 13 units, which is above $\mathrm { I } _ { 1 } \ = \ 9 .$ Therefore, a PM operation is performed following job 2 on machine 1. The processing of job 5 is suspended until the PM operation finishes at time 32. Meanwhile, the accumulated total processing time on machine 1 is reset after maintenance. The same rule is applied to all the machines, thus producing makespan of 64.
Fig. 3 shows the Gantt chart for a solution to the previous problem but taking PM operations into consideration during scheduling. The solution consists of a job sequence {8, 6, 3, 7, 1} in factory 0 and a job sequence {4, 9, 2, 0, 5} in factory 1. As we can see, the new solution of the optimization has less idle time and fewer PM operations. In addition, the makespan is now 51, which implies a decrease in the initial solution in Fig. 2 of 20.3%. The explanation is given by the fact that the solution with PM operations considered is usually different from the one if the PM operations are not considered (Ruiz et al., 2007).

## 4. The proposed multi-start iterated greedy algorithm In the literature, a high performing heuristic is often used to initialize the search for an IG algorithm. The main loop is to greedily repeat four operations (Ruiz & Stützle, 2007; Ruiz, Pan & Naderi, 2019): Utilize the destruction to partially destroy the candidate solution. For our problem, some jobs will be removed from the solution, resulting in an incomplete solution and a group of leftover jobs. Apply a greedy heuristic method to reinsert the removed jobs into the solution. A new complete solution will be generated in this con struction phase. Perform a local search to further optimize the new solution. Use a simulated annealing-like acceptance criterion with a constant temperature to determine whether the new solution is accepted. J.-y. In this study, we record the number of consecutive iterations c in which the solution has not been improved. The solution will be abandoned once c is larger than a specific threshold α. The algorithm then restarts from the heuristic initialization phase. Such a multi-start strat egy is adopted to prevent stagnation situations of the search due to insufficient diversification (Martí, Resende & Ribeiro, 2013). In the following, we describe the detailed phases of MSIG for PM/DPFSP.

## 4.1. Solution representation
To represent the job assignment to factories, a solution is represented by a two-dimensional array $\Pi = \{ \pi \sb { 1 } , \pi \sb { 2 } , . . . , \pi _ { F } \}$ }. There are F rows in the array, in which each row has a job sequence $\pi _ { f } ( f = 1 , 2 , . . . , F )$ consisting of a set of jobs assigned to the factory. Jobs in each sequence are sorted according to the processing order. For instance, the solution as shown in Fig. 3 can be represented as Π = {(8, 6, 3, 7, 1), (4, 9, 2, 0, 5)}. According to the PM strategy we take, once job sequences are determined, starting and ending times of PM operations on all machines are also fixed. So, there is no need to record PM operations in π . Such a sequence-based solution is widely used in the scheduling literature for its intuitive representation and convenience for programming (Arroyo, Leung & Tavares, 2019).

## 4.2. Heuristic method As for the initialization procedure, we propose an improved NEH2 heuristic method with dropout operation (INEH2\_dp for short) to pro duce a solution with a high level of quality. The NEH algorithm of Nawaz, Enscore and Ham (1983) has been regarded to be one of the most effective heuristic algorithms for the permutation flowshop scheduling problem (PFSP) with the makespan criterion (Ruiz & Maroto, 2005). Naderi and Ruiz (2010) extended NEH by considering the allocation of jobs to factories to fit for DPFSP and proposed the NEH1 and NEH2. The NEH2\_en of Ruiz, Pan and Naderi (2019) is a further improvement on the NEH2 method which increases the computational complexity to obtain a better performance. In the NEH2, all the jobs are first arranged in decreasing order of the total processing time on m machines $P _ { j } =$ $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { m } p _ { i , j } , \forall j \in N , } \end{array}$ resulting in the largest processing time (LPT) sequence. Then the jobs are orderly taken out from the sequence and placed at the best positions among all the F factories. The NEH2\_en improved the NEH2 heuristic in which after the position of a new job is fixed, either the job on its predecessor or successor is extracted at random and reinserted in the best positions in the same factory. Inspired by the NEH2\_en, we propose the INEH2\_dp method to fit our problem. The pseudo codes of INEH2\_dp are given in Fig. 4.
Procedure Destruction ( $\Pi=(\pi_{1},\pi_{2},..., \pi_{F})$ ) $\lambda_{d} := \varnothing$ for step := 1 to d do $f_{1}, f_{2} :=$ randomly select two factories if ( $C_{max}(\pi_{f_{1}}) > C_{max}(\pi_{f_{2}})$ ) then j := randomly remove one job from $\pi_{f_{1}}$ else j := randomly remove one job from $\pi_{f_{2}}$ endif Append job j to $\lambda_{d}$ endfor return $\lambda_{d}$ Fig 5. Procedure of the destruction phase.
In our INEH2\_dp heuristic method, the new job taken out from the LPT sequence is not greedily tested in all the positions in all the factories. Instead, each possible position has a certain probability k of being ignored. We refer to this operator and its probability k as dropout and dropout rate, where k is a parameter to be calibrated. The purpose of the dropout operator is to enhance some stochastics to our heuristic so that a different initial solution with a high level of quality can be generated when the algorithm restarts. In addition, the predecessor and successor of the inserted job are compared by $P _ { j } .$ We select the job with a smaller P and test to swap it with all the other jobs in the same factory. Finally, the swapping operator producing the least makespan is chosen. In the course of $C _ { m a x }$ calculation, each job on each machine in the sequence $\pi _ { f }$ is traversed one by one. There is an average of n/F jobs in each factory. This makes the complexity of $C _ { m a x }$ calculation in one fac tory equal to O(nm/F). INEH2\_dp evaluates a total of $[ n ( n + F ) / 2 ] { - } F$ schedules, which obtains the complexity of O(n3m/F). Note that the dropout operator does not change the framework of the proposed heu ristic, so it does not reduce the theoretical complexity.

Therefore, it makes sense to bias the destruction towards factories with larger makespan. The tournament selection is applied in the destruction operator. ## 4.4. Construction phase
As for the construction, we recombine the temporary sequence $\lambda _ { d }$ and the remaining partial solution π to reconstruct a new complete candidate solution. We found that the previously mentioned heuristic method can obtain good results with a little modification. Jobs in $\lambda _ { d }$ are rearranged by the total processing time $P _ { j } .$ We greedily insert the jobs into the best position among all the factories in the order of $P _ { j } ,$ from the largest to the smallest. Unlike in the INEH2\_dp, where the selected predecessor or successor is tested to swap with jobs in the corresponding factory, the construction operator tests to swap the selected job with all the jobs in all the factories. It is assumed that each factory has an average of n/F jobs, so the complexity of testing to insert one job into all the possible positions and to swap one job with all the jobs are both O(n<sup>2</sup>m/F). The complexity of the construction phase is O(n<sup>2</sup>md/F). The pseudo codes of construction phases are given in Fig. 6.

## 4.5. Local search methods
After the destruction and construction phases, a local search is per formed to further improve the solution. As to the permutation-based neighborhood structure, the swap and insertion operators are widely used in the local search phase (Fernandezviagas, Valente & Framinan, 2018). The swap operator is to interchange the positions of two jobs. The insertion operator removes a job from its original position and reinserts it into a different position. Based on the two operators, we propose three effective local search methods for the PM/DPFSP. The pseudo codes of the three local search methods are presented in Figs. 7–9, respectively.
Inter-factory Swap Local Search (ISLS): We test to swap each job in each factory in random order with the other jobs in the same factory. If an improvement swap is carried out, or all tests in a factory are completed, we end the search in the factory and begins the search in the next one. In the worst case where the solution is not improved, (n/F)(n/ F− 1)/2 swap operations will be tested in each factory. The ISLS termi nates after all the factories get the swap search done. Therefore, the complexity of the ISLS in all F factories is O(n<sup>3</sup>m/F<sup>2</sup>).
External-key-factory Swap Local Search (ESLS): In the PM/DPFSP, it is noted that makespan is determined by the factory with the largest makespan. Such a factory is referred to as the key factory, denoted as $f _ { k e y } .$ Jobs in $f _ { k e y }$ are picked up in a random order without repetition. Then we test to swap the selected job with all the other jobs in all the factories (including $f _ { k e y } )$ and then perform the best swap with the lowest $C _ { m a x } .$ The procedure terminates if an improvement is achieved, or all the jobs in $f _ { k e y }$ have been tested. It is assumed that there are averagely n/F jobs in $f _ { k e y } ,$ so $n ^ { 2 } / F$ swap operations will be tested at most. The complexity of ESLS is $O ( n ^ { 3 } m / \bar { F } ^ { 2 } )$ .
External-key-factory Insertion Local Search (EILS): Similar to the ESLL, the EILS tests to reinsert jobs in $f _ { k e y }$ in all the factories (including $f _ { k e y } )$ and conduct the best insertion in order to minimize the $C _ { m a x } .$ . Unlike ESLS, in which test of swapping jobs in two factories generates two new solutions and needs to calculate $C _ { m a x }$ result twice, the EILS only calcu lates one $C _ { m a x }$ result. Therefore, EILS shares the same complexity of O $( n ^ { 3 } m / F ^ { 2 } )$ with ESLS but theoretically has shorter computation time.
The local search phase is composed of the three proposed local search methods. It repeatedly calls the ISLS, the ESLS and the EILS until no better solution can be obtained. The pseudo codes of the complete local search procedures are presented in Fig. 10.

## 4.6. Acceptance criterion and restart strategy The acceptance criterion is designed to avoid local best solutions. After the destruction and construction phases and the local search phase, we apply a simulated annealing-like algorithm with constant tempera ture as an acceptance criterion. As is shown in the formula, a new so lution Π\* with a worse result than the current solution Π has a certain probability p to be accepted, so it is hopeful to abandon a local best solution and keep searching for better results. The constant temperature is based on the particular instance and it is computed following the formula suggested by Osman and Potts (1989). Despite of its simplicity, such an acceptance criterion has been widely used in scheduling prob lems (Pan et al., 2019; Ruiz & Stützle, 2007; Ruiz, Pan & Naderi, 2019). J.-y. Mao et al. ## 5. Experimental results In order to evaluate the algorithmic performance, we conducted numerical experiments. To the best of our knowledge, there is no existing instance of our problem. Therefore, we generated benchmarks based on the following parameters in Table 2. The value of $n ,$ m, F and $P _ { j o b }$ are set based on the studies of Taillard (1993) and Pan et al. (2019) to cover the instances of all the scales. We also referred to Ruiz et al. (2007) to set up parameters for the PM operation. The minimum value of T is set as 50 in case too short PM operation time has little impact on scheduling. The mean value of TPM is two times of that of the average $P _ { j o b } .$ . Meanwhile, in order to simplify the problem, the range of I is set 50% to 75% of the average total pro cessing time on each machine, so that only one PM operation is carried out on each machine during the whole manufacturing process. In total. there are 45 different combinations of the number of factories $F ,$ the number of machines m and the number of jobs n. Each combination randomly generates five different instances, which results in $4 5 \times 5 = 2 2 5$ instances of varying scales. We have coded all the al gorithms in $^ { \mathrm { C + + } }$ and compiled with Visual Studio 2019 with the x64 compiler with all optimization flags enable. All the experiments in this paper are performed on Windows Server 2012 on a PC with a Quad-core processor Intel E5-2640 2.4 GHz and 4 GB of RAM. The results of all the algorithms are measured by the relative percentage deviation (RPD) (Naderi & Ruiz, 2010; Ruiz & Stützle, 2007; Ruiz et al., 2007) and it is calculated as follows: $$ RPD = 100 \% \times \frac{Some_{sol} - Best_{sol}}{Best_{sol}}\tag{3} $$ where $S o m e _ { s o l }$ is the $C _ { m a x }$ obtained by a certain algorithm on a given instance and $B e s t _ { s o l }$ is the minimum $C _ { m a x }$ found in any experiment for the same instance. We carried out an analysis of variance (ANOVA) to determine whether the PRD results obtained by each algorithm are indeed significantly different. A 95% confidence level is employed in our experiments.

The stopping condition of an algorithm may be maximum compu tational time allowed, the maximum number of iterations, or the maximum number of two improvements. In this paper, a maximum elapsed CPU time, $t = C \times m \times n$ milliseconds, is set as the termination criterion, which has been commonly used in various scheduling prob lems (Pan et al., 2019). For the comparison experiments, we C = 50. The proposed MSIG has three parameters: the number of destructed jobs d, constant temperature coefficient T for the simulated annealinglike acceptance criterion and the number of trials α after which the so lution is restarted. We tested all reasonable combinations of k, d, T and α, where k = {0%,10%, 20%, 30%, 40%} d = {2, 3, 4, 5}, $T = = \{ 0 . 4 , 0 . 5 ,$ 0.6, 0.7, 0.8} and α = {700, 800, 900, 1000, 1100}. Each combination of parameters was repeated five times on a group of 45 instances covering all the combinations of the number of F, m and n. Following Ruiz and Stützle (2007), we analyzed the experimental data by ANOVA and finally set the parameters as follows: k = 10%, d = 3, T = 0.5 and α = 1000.

## 5.2. Comparison of proposed algorithms
To validate the performance of the proposed MSIG, we compared it against six state-of-the-art algorithms from the literature. These are: discrete differential evolution (DDE) algorithm (Zhang, Xing & Cao, 2018), hybrid genetic algorithm (HGA) (Huang et al., 2019), two stage iterated greedy (IG2S) algorithm (Ruiz, Pan & Naderi, 2019), iterated cocktail greedy (ICG) algorithm (Lin & Ying, 2016), improved discrete artificial bee colony (IDABC) algorithm (Mao et al., 2020a) and iterated greedy (IG) (Mao et al., 2020b) algorithm, where DDE, HGA, IG2S and ICG are not designed for PM/DPFSP, so we reconstruct them for our problem. Parameters of all algorithms are calibrated as done in MSIG and summarized in Table 4. According to the above literature, the three population-based algorithms (DDE, HGA and IDABC) and the three iteration-based algorithms (IG2S, ICG and IG) respectively possess excellent global exploration and outstanding local exploitation. There fore, they are selected to verify the proposed MSIG.
We perform five dependent runs for each algorithm to solve each of the 225 benchmarks with a given stop criterion t = 50 × m × n milli seconds. The average RPD of each instance size F|m|n is reported in Table 5. We also group the RPD values according to F, m and n in Table 6.
It can be clearly observed in Table 5 that the proposed MSIG per forms best among all the algorithms in comparison. The overall RPD values of all the algorithms, from the smallest to the largest, are respectively 0.225% of MSIG, 0.414% of IG, 0.553% of IDABC, 0.708% of IG2S, 0.768% of HGA, 3.409% of DDE and 3.492% of ICG. DDE and ICG perform much worse than the other algorithms. The bad results obtained by DDE and ICG can be explained by the lack of an effective local search mechanism. In addition, the MSIG performs best on 29 out of 45 instance sizes, which is far more than the 12 of IDABC, the seven of IG and the one of HGA. Table 6 illustrates that the MSIG obtains the best result for almost all the groups with regarding to different numbers of factories F, different numbers of machines m and different numbers of jobs n, except for n = 100, in which average RPD of IG is slightly smaller

than that of MSIG.
In addition, Table 7 concludes a t-test with a significance level equal to 5% for all the results yielded by each pair of the algorithms. According to Table 7, it is clear that there is no significant difference between the pair of HGA and IG2S and the pair of DDE and ICG. All the other algo rithm pairs generate significantly different results. Therefore, we can divide the algorithms into five homogenous groups, with no significant differences within each group. In order of average RPD values, from the smallest to the largest, the groups are sorted as follows: {MSIG}, {IG}, {IDABC}, {IG2S, HGA}, and {DDE, ICG}.
In Fig. 13, we count the number of best solutions of each instance obtained by each algorithm. It can be observed that the MSIG generates the most number of best solutions among all the competitive algorithms. There are 146 best solutions generated by MSIG out of a total of 225 instances. Though IG is significantly better than IDABC in terms of average RPD results, they are tied for second place with 68 best solu tions. IG2S, HGA, DDE and ICG generate 36, 31, 8 and 8 best solutions respectively.
Fig. 14 shows the average RPD values generated by all the algorithms at the elapsed CPU time $t = 5 0 \times m \times n$ milliseconds. We record the makespan of the best solution over a period of $5 \times m \times 1$ n milliseconds to provide an overall picture of the algorithms. Meanwhile, following Zou et al. (Zou et al., 2020) and many others, a multifactor ANOVA is carried out to confirm whether the RPD values of each algorithm at each moment are indeed significantly different. As can be seen, the mean plots show that the proposed MSIG performs significantly better than the other algorithms all the time throughout the progress. DDE and ICG have the worst optimizations of all the algorithms because their RPD results are the largest and decrease very little as computational time increases. Furthermore, DDE and ICG have more parameters than the others, which increases calibration complexity. IG performs a bit worse than IDABC at the beginning, but it statistically exceeds IDABC after 35 × m × n milliseconds and further expands the gap between them as time goes on. Throughout the whole process, there is no significant difference between the RPD results of HGA and IG2S.
Next, we plot the interactions of algorithms type and the parameters of instances $F ,$ m and n in Figs. 15 and 16 based on the RPD results at t = $5 0 \times m \times n$ milliseconds. The results are again analyzed by ANOVA where $F , m ,$ and n are considered as non-controllable factors. DDE and ICG are removed from these plots as they are clearly worse than the other algorithms. We can see that when the number of factories F and the number of machines m change, the average RPD values of each algo rithm have the same changing trend, while the MSIG has the minimum variation. In other words, it is proved that MSIG has better robustness for the instances of a different scale than the other competitive algorithms. Fig. 16 shows that the population-based algorithms, HGA and IDABC, perform relatively poorly in the small-scale n of the instances while get better rapidly as n increases. When n increases to 500, HGA gains no significantly worse RPD results than the overall second-best IG. And IDABC even far exceeds IG. By contrast, the greedy iteration-based al gorithms, MSIG, IG and IG2S, generate more stable RPD results when n changes. In general, the proposed MSIG is superior to the other compared algorithms in terms of both RPD results and stability when the parameters of instances change.
Finally, it can be safely summarized that the MSIG is the most effective algorithm for solving the PM/DPFSP with makespan criterion among all the compared algorithms. The MSIG outperforms the other algorithms in terms of both RPD results and robustness.

## 6. Conclusions and future research
Distributed scheduling in multi-factory production has been a hot research topic in the past decades. However, scheduling problems with PM operations are seldom investigated. In this study, the distributed permutation flowshop scheduling problem with preventive maintenance (PM/DPFSP) is considered. We proposed a simple but effective multistart iterated greedy (MSIG) to minimize the makespan. The MSIG uses an improved NEH2 heuristic algorithm with a dropout operation to initialize the solution. After that, destruction and construction phases are greedily iterated. During the destruction phase, a couple of jobs are removed from the complete candidate solution. After that, the con struction phase applies a constructive heuristic to reconstruct the solu tion. In attempting to obtain optimal solutions, a local search basing on insertion and swap operations is also presented. Once a feasible solution is completed, an acceptance criterion determines whether the incum bent solution will be replaced by the new one. In addition, a solution will be abandon after a certain number of iterations without improvement. Then the algorithm restarts with the heuristic method. We carried out experiments based on randomly generated instances to evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed MSIG. The experimental results have indicated that the MSIG performs much better than the existing algo rithms in the literature.
In the near future, we will still focus on PM/DPFSP. Despite the avoidance of the remaining local optima, the multi-start strategy does not take full advantage of existing solutions. We are going to further study the restarting method to promote efficiency. In addition, we are also interested in other objectives in PM/DPFSP (e.g. total flow time, total tardiness) which are common in practice.
